summary:
We developed a monolithic space health-monitoring web application featuring a main crew dashboard and a portable device (PDA) interface, backed by NASA research, OSDR studies, and GeneLab/ALSDA datasets. The main app provides continuous multi-crew tracking, organic sample analysis (such as blood and urine), extended health descriptions, care instructions, mental assessments, and hands-free gesture controls. For out-of-base operations, the portable version monitors vital short-term parameters-including blood oxygen, ECG, blood pressure, glucose, insulin, breathing rate, temperature, hydration, and radiation dose-triggering color-coded alerts (red for the user, yellow for crewmates) when readings deviate from normal distributions.

The application addresses space healthcare challenges by dynamically adjusting physiological norms based on mission environment, sex, and baseline health, while tracking long-term health metrics and emergencies like CO2 buildup or depressurization. This proactive, prevention-focused monitoring is critical because extended missions expose astronauts to severe hazards-such as radiation, cardiovascular deconditioning, bone and muscle loss, psychiatric stress, and Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-Ocular Syndrome-requiring early anomaly detection to safeguard crew health far from Earth.
details:
Our project is a comprehensive, monolithic space health-monitoring web application built with TypeScript-developed using laptops and tablets-that is designed to support astronauts by evaluating both their physical and mental well-being in space. Backed by NASA research, OSDR studies, and GeneLab/ALSDA datasets, the system periodically receives biometric data from wearable and environmental sensors, supplemented by quick physical and mental health tests as well as organic sample analysis (such as blood, urine, and sperm). It evaluates this combined information against tailored normal-distribution norms specifically preset for different space environments (spacecraft, stations, Moon, or Mars), biological sex, and each astronaut's initial baseline health.

Based on this analysis, the main application-intended to be projected onto a large display inside the spacecraft-provides continuous multi-crew tracking, extended health descriptions, care instructions, and intuitive feedback with general wellness recommendations. For out-of-base operations, compact portable wearable devices (PDAs) monitor vital short-term parameters-including blood oxygen, ECG, blood pressure, glucose, insulin, breathing rate, temperature, hydration, and radiation dose-triggering immediate color-coded warnings (red for the user and yellow for crewmates) if any health metrics deviate significantly from safe thresholds.

A key creative feature of our solution is its 100% hands-free spatial gesture and voice-based interface, specifically designed around zero-gravity ergonomics to allow effortless interaction with the main screen without traditional peripherals. Looking ahead, our future considerations focus on implementing mental health tests to improve psychological well-being through appropriate interventions (such as doctor consultations, calls home, or medication), deploying portable devices capable of displaying real-time warnings in any environment outside the space station, dynamically adjusting health parameter norms according to the previous biological history of each specific astronaut, and incorporating additional health parameters with deeper analysis to provide more reliable health insights. This proactive, prevention-focused monitoring is critical because extended missions expose astronauts to severe hazards-such as radiation, cardiovascular deconditioning, bone and muscle loss, psychiatric stress, Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-Ocular Syndrome, and emergencies like CO2 buildup or depressurization. Ultimately, by pairing automated sensor tracking and environment-specific health benchmarks with dual-screen accessibility, Lumio Solstice aims to reduce crew cognitive load, speed up medical response, and improve overall astronaut safety and mission success far from Earth.
